summary: Taft sits at the southwestern edge of the San Joaquin Valley where the flat, sun-baked oil fields meet the Temblor Range foothills, and its entire existence traces back to one resource: petroleum. The Midway-Sunset oil field — one of the largest in the United States — still defines the local economy, with pumpjacks dotting the landscape in nearly every direction and oil-sector jobs anchoring employment in a way few California cities still experience. That single-industry concentration shows up in the housing math: a median home value of $246,400 against a median household income of $64,479 yields a price-to-income ratio under 4:1, making homeownership arithmetically plausible in a state where ratios of 8:1 or 10:1 are common. Rent at $989 a month reinforces that affordability, though the tradeoff is isolation — Bakersfield is roughly 45 minutes east, and there's no freeway running through town, just two-lane highways crossing arid terrain under nearly ten hours of daily sunshine year-round. The town grid is compact and low-slung, with a small commercial stretch along Center Street, a community college campus (Taft College), and Buena Vista Lake bed to the north — now dry farmland, not recreation. With 78°F average highs, summers are genuinely hot and winters mild, but the landscape is stark brown hills and scrub, not green valleys. Taft is a place where California's oil past and affordable-housing present coexist on the same dusty ground, and neither is going anywhere fast.
